text:
customer_jdoe: Heads-up — after migrating a service to Private VPC we started seeing streaming requests drop around 55-65s. Client gets a 504 + socket closed. No app errors, just TLS/connection resets on our side. Request id: r-0a1b2c3d.

sara_support: Sorry you're hitting this — is this HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming or HTTP/2? region and whether you put a NAT/GW in front? Any sample curl or logs you can paste?

customer_jdoe: It's chunked HTTP/1.1 (Transfer-Encoding: chunked). We do have a NAT gateway for egress. Quick server log snippet: 
```
[2026-02-28T12:34:55Z] request r-0a1b2c3d stream started
[2026-02-28T12:35:50Z] TLS alert: unexpected_message, connection reset by peer
```
We also ran a client-side tcpdump and saw the server stop responding after ~60s.

ben_infra: That pattern smells like an egress return-path / ephemeral port issue (NACL or stateful rule mismatch). Can you paste the subnet's NACL rules + the instance SG outbound? Also which OS kernel (some kernels randomize ephemeral ranges differently).

customer_jdoe: NACL on the Private subnet (copied):
```
Rule  10  ALLOW  IN  TCP  80  0.0.0.0/0
Rule  20  ALLOW  IN  TCP  443 0.0.0.0/0
Rule  30  DENY   OUT TCP  32768-65535 0.0.0.0/0
Rule 100  ALLOW  OUT TCP  80,443 0.0.0.0/0
```
SG outbound: Allow all (0.0.0.0/0) TCP 0-65535.

ben_infra: There's the culprit — stateless NACL rule 30 denies outbound ephemeral ports. NACLs are evaluated by rule number order; a DENY earlier will drop traffic before your later ALLOW. Because NACLs are stateless the return packets won't be auto-allowed. That leads to the established TCP state being broken after the ephemeral port is used for return traffic.

amy_ops: Confirmed with tcpdump (host side):
```
12:34:56.789 IP client.54321 > backend.443: Flags [S]
12:34:56.789 IP backend.443 > client.54321: Flags [S.]
12:35:55.001 IP 169.254.169.254 > client.54321: RST  <-- unexpected RST/ICMP coming from egress path
```
Looks like the NAT/NACL dropped/rewrote the flow causing a reset.

ben_infra: Two remediation paths:
- Preferred: Remove/adjust the DENY rule. Add explicit allow for ephemeral range (32768-65535) both IN/OUT with a rule number lower than the DENY, or delete the DENY entirely.
- Alternative: Move outbound through a stateful SG+NAT setup (SGs are stateful so return traffic isn't blocked). Also check NAT gateway connection tracking limits if you have very high concurrency.

sara_support: For quick repro steps we recommend:
1) On a test instance in the same subnet run: `nc -l 443` and stream a long payload.
2) From an external client do a streaming POST with chunked Transfer-Encoding and measure when connection drops.
3) Toggle NACL rule (temporarily allow ephemeral range) and re-run. If stable -> NACL was the cause.

customer_jdoe: We added an ALLOW OUT rule (rule 25) for TCP 32768-65535 and also added corresponding IN allow. After applying it streams have stayed up for 24h with no resets.

ben_infra: Great — please also:
- Ensure rule numbering is consistent across both subnet NACLs (subnet-level NACLs apply to both directions).
- Consider shrinking the ephemeral range if your OS/kernel supports it, or align with AWS recommendations (1024-65535 is typical) to make auditing easier.
- If you expect >10k concurrent connections, monitor NAT GW connection tracking and scale/HA accordingly.

amy_ops: Filing a short runbook note: `support-runbooks/firewall-nacl-ephemeral-issue` (internal) — will include the tcpdump snippet and the `aws ec2 describe-network-acls` filters. infra-bot: created ticket INC-2982.

customer_jdoe: Thanks team — huge help. We'll leave the ALLOW in place and tighten later. :tada:
